title: Sewer Socialism for Schools
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman offers incoming governors a list of practical education ideas sorted by cost, arguing that without a single "weird trick" the job is good old-fashioned leadership, incrementalism and evaluation. He frames the approach as "sewer socialism," meaning fix the potholes of public education for ordinary students and families. The no-cost items include opting in to more state-level NAEP data, returning test results to parents within 30 days, adding science to accountability systems, automatic enrollment in advanced courses, and campaigns that celebrate school success. Low and medium cost ideas include an England-style phonics check for six-year-olds, North Carolina's Advanced Teacher Roles, and developing social studies tests so that knowledge-building is signalled and measured. The through-line is that a governor mainly signals that education matters through messaging, staffing and budget, then delivers measurable basics.
points: Aldeman sorts reforms by cost (no-cost, low-cost, medium-cost), which makes the list usable as a first-year governor's agenda.
Several no-cost moves are about information: opt in to more NAEP data, publish results within 30 days, and count science in accountability.
A simple phonics check, modeled on England's 40-word test, would give states an early metric for their science-of-reading investments.
Advanced Teacher Roles (team teaching, as in Opportunity Culture) is offered as the cautious alternative to another round of teacher-evaluation reform.
Social studies and science assessments matter because critical thinking needs a base of broad knowledge to work on.
quotes: From my perspective, the most important thing a governor can do is signal that education matters, and to make that evident through their messaging, their staffing, and their budget.

But eventually they have shift from campaigning to governing, and for that, the best advice I have is to focus on making public education work better, for ordinary students and families, and focusing on delivering on that promise.
Instead, I think we need some good old-fashioned leadership and a heavy dose of incrementalism and evaluation.

Despite much of the testing infrastructure shifting online, states are taking longer than ever to share the results. This is ridiculous and undermines the utility of having common, standardized benchmarks in the first place.
By leaving science results out of their accountability systems, states are missing an opportunity to show that they value science as an important academic subject beyond reading and math.
A phonics check is not fancy or costly, and it requires only about five minutes per child to administer, but it accomplishes two things.
Instead of one teacher being in charge of one isolated classroom, these schools have teachers work in small teams that are responsible for a larger group of kids.
Helping students become “critical thinkers” may sound good as a talking point, but students need a foundation of knowledge to think critically about.
